Rayst men mikh bay di palis — Hirsh Ber — es iz do a Got oyf der velt! [They pull me by the corners of my garment — Hirsh Ber — there IS a G-d in the world!]

And our master z"l was careful not to say Torah before them — and when they came in the middle he would steer toward another matter. And to R. Naftali he said: he should speak only with Landa — and with Hirsh Ber not at all. And to R. Nussun z"l he said: he should speak with Hirsh Ber. And once our master z"l told him to tell them a story from the Baal Shem Tov z"l. And Moharan"as z"l was surprised in his heart — had he not heard from our master z"l to be careful not to say Torah before them? Our master z"l answered: "What did I say?" —

Vos hob ikh gezugt? — "Sapru vagoyim es kvodo." [What did I say? — "Tell among the nations His glory."]

And at the beginning of our master's z"l coming to Uman — they considered him wise but not like their teacher "Vizel." Afterwards they considered him wise as he. And afterwards — when they came to know he was wiser than he. And they had a question from their teacher mentioned above — and had no answer. And they went regarding this to our master z"l to ask him. And immediately when they entered his house — our master z"l posed this very question and answered them with a correct answer. And they were very astonished — and kissed the feet of our master z"l and said to him: "Fair enough — we know you are wiser than Vizel — for he had no answer and you have an answer — but how did you know our thought?" He answered and explained to them that this is from wisdom — for whoever has a clean and clear mind can recognize the thought through the hairs. And they accepted this. But afterwards when they left him they were still more astonished and said: "Us! Such wise men as we — he could mislead so greatly — surely this is impossible by human intellect in any manner etc."

aligned_segments.he:
ג- מַעֲשֶׂה מִקַּאפְּצִין פָּאשָׁא
מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁסִּפֵּר אַדְמוֹ"ר מִקַּאפְּצִין פָּאשָׁא
פַּעַם אַחַת הָיָה אֵצֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ הַתּוֹגָר אִישׁ אֶחָד מֵאַחֵינוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהָיָה חָשׁוּב בְּעֵינָיו מְאֹד מִכָּל שָׂרֵי הַמְּלוּכָה אֲשֶׁר לוֹ, וַיֶּאֱהָבֵהוּ אַהֲבָה גְּדוֹלָה וַעֲצוּמָה מְאֹד יוֹתֵר מִכָּל שָׂרֵי הַמְּלוּכָה אֲשֶׁר לוֹ. וּבְכָל יוֹם וָיוֹם הָיָה קוֹרֵא אוֹתוֹ לְבֵיתוֹ לְהִשְׁתַּעְשֵׁעַ עִמּוֹ יַחַד. וַיְקַנְּאוּ בּוֹ שָׂרֵי הַמְּלוּכָה, וְחָשְׁבוּ מַחֲשָׁבוֹת לְהַעֲלִיל עָלָיו לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ וִיאַבְּדוּהוּ מִן הָעוֹלָם. וְהָיָה בֵּינֵיהֶם פָּאשָׁא אֶחָד שֶׁהָיָה נִקְרָא קַאפְּצִין פָּאשָׁא, שֶׁשִּׂנְאָתוֹ לְהַיִּשְׂרָאֵל הַזֶּה הָיְתָה גְּדוֹלָה יוֹתֵר מִכָּל הַשָּׂרִים. וְלִפְנֵי הַיִּשְׂרָאֵל הֶרְאָה עַצְמוֹ כְּאוֹהֵב לוֹ, וּבְכָל יוֹם חָשַׁב מַחֲשָׁבוֹת חֶפְצוֹ שֶׁיַּצְלִיחַ בְּיָדוֹ לִמְצֹא עָלָיו אֵיזֶה עֲלִילָה לִפְנֵי
הַמֶּלֶךְ.
פַּעַם אַחַת בָּא הַפָּאשָׁא הַנַּ"ל לְהַיִּשְׂרָאֵל הַנַּ"ל, וְהִתְחִיל לְדַבֵּר עִמּוֹ בְּעָרְמָה, וַיְסַפֵּר לוֹ בַּאֲשֶׁר שֶׁהָיָה אֵצֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ, וְשָׁמַע מִפִּיו אֵיךְ שֶׁהוּא אוֹהֵב אוֹתְךָ, אַךְ יֵשׁ לוֹ יִסּוּרִים מִדָּבָר אֶחָד, כִּי כְּשֶׁאַתָּה בָּא לְפָנָיו לְדַבֵּר אִתּוֹ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לִסְבֹּל רֵיחַ פִּיךָ, כִּי הוּא מַרְגִּישׁ רֵיחַ רַע נוֹדֵף מִפִּיךָ, וְהוּא אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת בִּלְעָדֶיךָ, וְיֵשׁ לוֹ יִסּוּרִים גְּדוֹלִים מִזֶּה, לָזֹאת עֲצָתִי כִּי בְּכָל עֵת שֶׁתָּבוֹא לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, תֹּאחֵז מִטְפַּחַת עִם בְּשָׂמִים לִפְנֵי פִּיךָ, כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יַרְגִּישׁ הַמֶּלֶךְ הָרֵיחַ הָרָע מִפִּיךָ, כִּי הַבְּשָׂמִים יְבַטְּלוּ הָרֵיחַ רַע לְמַעַן לֹא תִּבְאַשׁ בְּעֵינֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ. וְהַיִּשְׂרָאֵל הַנַּ"ל מֵחֲמַת תְּמִימוּתוֹ הֶאֱמִין לִדְבָרָיו, וְנִסְכַּם
בְּדַעְתּוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן.
אַחַר־כָּךְ הָלַךְ הַפָּאשָׁא הַנַּ"ל אֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ וַיְסַפֵּר לוֹ כִּי שָׁמַע מֵהַיִּשְׂרָאֵל הַנַּ"ל, שֶׁאָמַר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ יִסּוּרִים גְּדוֹלִים, כִּי בְּכָל עֵת שֶׁמְּדַבֵּר עִם הַמֶּלֶךְ מַרְגִּישׁ רֵיחַ רַע יוֹצֵא מִפִּי הַמֶּלֶךְ, עַל כֵּן נִסְכַּם עֲצָתוֹ כְּשֶׁיָּבוֹא לְדַבֵּר עִמְּךָ, אֲדוֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ, יֹאחֵז מִטְפַּחַת עִם בְּשָׂמִים נֶגֶד פִּיו כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יַרְגִּישׁ רֵיחַ רַע מִפִּי הַמֶּלֶךְ, וְזֶה לְךָ הָאוֹת כִּי כֵּנִים דְּבָרַי, כִּי לְמָחָר כַּאֲשֶׁר יָבֹא לְדַבֵּר עִמְּךָ תִּרְאֶה בְּעֵינֶיךָ שֶׁיֹּאחֵז אֶת הַמִּטְפַּחַת נֶגֶד פִּיו. כְּשֶׁשָּׁמַע זֹאת הַמֶּלֶךְ נִתְכַּעֵס מְאֹד, וְאָמַר לוֹ כְּשֶׁאֶרְאֶה אֲשֶׁר
כֵּנִים דְּבָרֶיךָ אָז אֲאַבֵּד אוֹתוֹ מִן הָעוֹלָם.
וְהִנֵּה הַיִּשְׂרָאֵל הַנַּ"ל בָּא בְּיוֹם מָחָר לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, וַיֹּאחֵז הַמִּטְפַּחַת נֶגֶד פִּיו כַּאֲשֶׁר יָעַץ לוֹ הַפָּאשָׁא, כִּי הֶאֱמִין לִדְבָרָיו. וְהַמֶּלֶךְ כְּשֶׁרָאָה זֹאת וַיִּוָּכַח לָדַעַת כִּי כֵּנִים הֵם דִּבְרֵי הַפָּאשָׁא, תֵּכֶף כָּתַב מִכְתָּב כַּדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה, "כַּאֲשֶׁר יָבֹא הָאִישׁ הַמּוֹסֵר כְּתַב זֶה לִפְנֵיכֶם תַּשְׁלִיכוּ אוֹתוֹ תֵּכֶף לְכִבְשַׁן הָאֵשׁ אֲשֶׁר כָּל חַיָּבֵי מִיתוֹת נִשְׂרָפִים שָׁם". וְהַמֶּלֶךְ חָתַם אֶת הַמִּכְתָּב בְּחוֹתָמוֹ, וְאָמַר לְזֶה הָאִישׁ, אֲבַקֵּשׁ מִמְּךָ שֶׁאַתָּה בְּעַצְמְךָ תָּבִיא אֶת הַמִּכְתָּב הַזֶּה לְהָאִישׁ שֶׁנִּכְתַּב עַל הָאַדְרֶעס (הַכְּתֹבֶת) שֶׁהוּא בְּמָקוֹם פְּלוֹנִי. וְהַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי הַנַּ"ל לָקַח הַמִּכְתָּב, וְהִבְטִיחַ לַמֶּלֶךְ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה כִּדְבָרָיו. וְלֹא יָדַע מַה כָּתוּב בּוֹ וְהָלַךְ לְבֵיתוֹ. וְהִנֵּה זֶה הָאִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל הַנַּ"ל, הָיָה מַחֲזִיק מְאֹד בְּמִצְוָה לָמוּל יַלְדֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּבְכָל עֵת שֶׁכִּבְּדוּהוּ בְּמִצְוַת חִתּוּךְ, לֹא פָּנָה אֶל שׁוּם מְנִיעָה שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ כִּי הַמִּצְוָה הָיְתָה יְקָרָה בְּעֵינָיו מְאֹד. וְאָז בְּאוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם שֶׁהָיָה צָרִיךְ לִנְסֹעַ לִמְסֹר הַמִּכְתָּב מֵהַמֶּלֶךְ לַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁלַח, וַה' אֲשֶׁר חָפֵץ לְהַצִּיל יְדִידוֹ הַנֶּאֱמָן, סִבֵּב שֶׁבָּא אֶחָד מִכְּפָר אֶחָד וְכִבְּדוֹ שֶׁיִּסַּע עִמּוֹ לְהַכְּפָר וְלָמוּל אֶת בְּנוֹ. וּמֵחֲמַת כִּי דַּרְכּוֹ הָיָה לִבְלִי לְהַנִּיחַ אֶת הַמִּצְוָה הַזֹּאת בְּשׁוּם אֹפֶן, הִתְחִיל לַחְשֹׁב מָה אֶעֱשֶׂה לְצִוּוּי הַמֶּלֶךְ בִּדְבַר מִכְתָּבוֹ. וְסִבֵּב ה' שֶׁבָּא לְנֶגְדּוֹ הַפָּאשָׁא הַנַּ"ל. וַיְסַפֵּר לְהַפָּאשָׁא שֶׁהָיָה אֵצֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ, וְהַמֶּלֶךְ מָסַר לוֹ מִכְתָּב שֶׁיִּמְסְרֵהוּ לְהָאִישׁ שֶׁנִּשְׁלַח לוֹ, וְהַיּוֹם הִזְמִין לוֹ ה' מִצְוַת חִתּוּךְ, וְדַרְכִּי לִבְלִי לְהַנִּיחַ אֶת הַמִּצְוָה הַזֹּאת בְּשׁוּם אֹפֶן, עַל־כֵּן אֲנִי מְבַקֵּשׁ מִמְּךָ שֶׁתִּקַּח אֶת הַמִּכְתָּב וְתוֹלִיךְ אוֹתוֹ לְשָׁם. וְהִנֵּה הַפָּאשָׁא הַנַּ"ל שָׂמַח מְאֹד, כִּי עַתָּה יוּכַל לְהַלְשִׁין עָלָיו עוֹד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, כִּי לֹא עָשָׂה רְצוֹן הַמֶּלֶךְ עִם הַמִּכְתָּב. וַיִּקַּח הַפָּאשָׁא הַמִּכְתָּב מִיָּדוֹ וּמְסָרוֹ לְזֶה הָאִישׁ שֶׁנִּשְׁלַח אֵלָיו. וְזֶה הָיָה מְמֻנֶּה לִשְׂרֹף הַחַיָּבֵי מִיתוֹת שֶׁל הַמֶּלֶךְ וְתֵכֶף חָטַף אֶת הַפָּאשָׁא הַנַּ"ל וַיִּזְרֹק אוֹתוֹ לְתוֹךְ כִּבְשַׁן הָאֵשׁ
וְנִשְׂרַף, כַּאֲשֶׁר מַגִּיעַ מִשְׁפָּטוֹ עַל פִּי ה' מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה.
וְהִנֵּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי לֹא יָדַע כְּלָל מֵהַנַּ"ל שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה לוֹ, לְמָחָר חָזַר וּבָא לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ. וּכְשֶׁרָאָה אוֹתוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ תָּמַהּ מְאֹד, וְאָמַר לוֹ הַעוֹד לֹא מָסַרְתָּ אֶת הַמִּכְתָּב שֶׁנָּתַתִּי בְּיָדְךָ לְהָאִישׁ הַנַּ"ל. הֵשִׁיב לוֹ אֲדוֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ אֶת הַמִּכְתָּב מָסַרְתִּי לְקַאפְּצִין פָּאשָׁא הַנַּ"ל, שֶׁהוּא יִמְסְרֶנָּה לְהָאִישׁ, יַעַן כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִזְמִין לִי מִצְוַת חִתּוּךְ, וְדַרְכִּי לִבְלִי לְהַנִּיחַ אֶת הַמִּצְוָה הַזֹּאת. אָז הֵבִין הַמֶּלֶךְ הֲלֹא דָּבָר הוּא שֶׁיִּשָּׂרֵף זֶה הַפָּאשָׁא שֶׁהִלְשִׁין עָלָיו לְפָנָיו. וְשָׁאַל הַמֶּלֶךְ תֵּכֶף אֶת הָאִישׁ, מַה זֶּה שֶׁאַתָּה אוֹחֵז מִטְפַּחַת עִם בְּשָׂמִים נֶגֶד פִּיךָ בְּעֵת שֶׁאַתָּה מְדַבֵּר עִמִּי. הֵשִׁיב לוֹ שֶׁהַפָּאשָׁא נָתַן לוֹ עֵצָה הַזֹּאת, כִּי אָמַר לִי שֶׁשָּׁמַע מִמְּךָ שֶׁאֵינְךָ יָכוֹל לִסְבֹּל רֵיחַ פִּי. אָז סִפֵּר לוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ אֵיךְ שֶׁהַפָּאשָׁא הִלְשִׁין עָלָיו לְפָנָיו שֶׁאָמַרְתָּ לוֹ שֶׁאֵינְךָ יָכוֹל לִסְבֹּל רֵיחַ פִּי, וְעַל כֵּן תֹּאחֵז מִטְפַּחַת עִם בְּשָׂמִים שֶׁלֹּא תַּרְגִּישׁ רֵיחַ רַע מִפִּי. וַיְסַפֵּר לוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ מַה שֶּׁהָיָה כָּתוּב בְּהַמִּכְתָּב שֶׁנָּתַן לוֹ, וְאָמַר לוֹ עַתָּה אֲנִי יוֹדֵע אֲשֶׁר ה' הַשַּׁלִּיט בָּאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר מַצִּיל יְדִידָיו מִכָּל רַע, וּלְהַפָּאשָׁא הַנַּ"ל כַּאֲשֶׁר זָמַם לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּךָ, כֵּן נַעֲשָׂה לוֹ, וַיָּשֶׁב לוֹ ה' גְּמוּלוֹ בְּרֹאשׁוֹ. וּמֵאָז וָהָלְאָה נִתְגַּדֵּל בַּחֲשִׁיבוּתוֹ בְּעֵינֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ יוֹתֵר מִכָּל הַשָּׂרִים אֲשֶׁר
אִתּוֹ, וְהָיָה חָשׁוּב וְיָקָר בְּעֵינָיו מְאֹד מְאֹד.
aligned_segments.en:
And once our master z"l came to them and they had a book in the Greek language — and our master z"l asked them: What is this? And they answered him dismissively: this is not for you. So it was several times that he asked them and they answered as mentioned. And he took it in his hand and grasped some pages of the book — and told them by heart what was written there — also the page and the line. And they were very astonished. In sum — they became deeply attached to him — and his love entered their hearts greatly from the immensity of his wisdom z"l. And they were accustomed to enter to him — and he was held in very great esteem in their eyes. And once they spoke of Mashiach — they answered and said: "We want you to be Mashiach." And once they said to him: "If the old Emperor were still alive — he would take the royal crown from his own head and crown you because of your awesome wisdom. But what can we do — this king is a fool etc."

Once they played chess at our master's z"l — and the way of chess is that during the game one forgets the awe of honor — and they became quite informal. And they did not have such great awe of him z"l. And in the middle — R. Nussun and R. Naftali entered the house with awe and reverence as was customary. And when they [the heretics] saw this — they became deflated. Our master z"l answered and said to them: You are not my army. And he told them a story: that once a king took his friend to a private room and played chess with him — and the way etc. as mentioned — and the king forgot he was a king. And likewise the friend forgot he was playing with the king — and they played like two simple men — sometimes the king won and sometimes the friend won etc. — and the awe was somewhat forgotten. And at this time certain ministers of the realm were needed by the king — and they entered with awe and reverence as was customary. And the friend began to look at himself: Is he not playing with the king? And he did not play well — since he did not want to beat the king. And the king said to him: what is this? This is not your business —

Mit zey fir ikh lender, un mit dir shpil ikh Shach. [With them I rule countries — and with you I play chess.]

aligned_segments.he:
ד- מַעֲשֶׂה מִמָּטָר
מַעֲשֶׂה מִמָּטָר, מֵעִנְיָן שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִכְבֹּשׁ הַמִּלְחָמָה רַק עִם הַפְּשׁוּטִים אוֹמְרֵי תְּהִלִּים בִּפְשִׁיטוּת וְכוּ' וְלֹא עִם הַהוֹלְכִים בְּחָכְמוֹת. סִפֵּר רַבֵּנוּ זַ"ל מָשָׁל מִמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁהָלַךְ לָצוּד חַיּוֹת (נאוולאוי) וְנָסַע לָבוּשׁ כְּאִישׁ פָּשׁוּט, כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נָקֵל לְהַצְּחוֹק. וּבְאֶמְצַע פִּתְאֹם יָרַד מָטָר גָּדוֹל מַמָּשׁ מַבּוּל מַיִם, וְכָל הַשָּׂרֵי מְלוּכָה נִתְפַּזְּרוּ אֶחָד לְאֶחָד וְכוּ'. וְהַמֶּלֶךְ הָיָה בְּסַכָּנָה גְּדוֹלָה, וְחִפֵּשׂ עַד שֶׁמָּצָא בַּיִת כַּפְרִי אֶחָד. וְהָיָה שָׁם אִישׁ כַּפְרִי, וְלָקַח אֶת הַמֶּלֶךְ וְהִלְבִּישׁוֹ, וְנָתַן לוֹ אֲכִילָה שֶׁלּוֹ גְּרִיץ (מְרַק גְּרִיסִים) וְכוּ', וְהִסִּיק אֶת הַתַּנּוּר, וְהִנִּיחוֹ לִישֹׁן עַל הַפִּיעֶקְלִיק (סָמוּךְ לַתַּנוּר) וְכוּ'. וְכָל־כָּךְ הָיָה עָרֵב וּמָתוֹק לְהַמֶּלֶךְ, שֶׁמֵּעוֹלָם לֹא טָעַם טַעַם עָרֵב כָּזֶה, כִּי הָיָה עָיֵף וְיָגֵעַ וְכוּ'. וְהַשָּׂרֵי מְלוּכָה חִפְּשׂוּ אֶת הַמֶּלֶךְ עַד שֶׁבָּאוּ לְשָׁם, וְרָאוּ שֶׁהוּא יָשֵׁן. וְרָצוּ שֶׁיַּחֲזֹר הַמֶּלֶךְ לְבֵיתוֹ עִמָּהֶם. וְאָמַר לָהֶם, כֵּיוָן שֶׁאַתֶּם לֹא הִצַּלְתֶּם אוֹתִי וְכָל אֶחָד נִתְפַּזֵּר לְהַצִּיל אֶת עַצְמוֹ, וְזֶה הִצִּיל אוֹתִי, וּפֹה טָעַמְתִּי טַעַם מָתוֹק כָּזֶה, עַל־כֵּן הוּא יָבִיא אוֹתִי בָּעֲגָלָה שֶׁלּוֹ וּבְאֵלּוּ הַמַּלְבּוּשִׁים, וְהוּא יוֹשִׁיב
אוֹתִי עַל כִּסֵּא הַמְּלוּכָה.
וְסִיֵּם עַל זֶה רַבֵּנוּ זַ"ל כַּאֲשֶׁר מוּבָא שֶׁבְּעִקְּבוֹת מְשִׁיחָא יִהְיֶה מַבּוּל "מֶען וֶועט שִׁיסֶען מִיט אֶפִּיקוֹרְסוּת" (יִירוּ עִם אֶפִּיקוֹרְסוּת) לֹא שֶׁל מַיִם, רַק שֶׁל מַחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת. וִיכֻסּוּ כָּל הֶהָרִים הַגְּבוֹהִים, וַאֲפִלּוּ בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה מַבּוּל, רַק מֵחֲמַת שֶׁהָלַךְ בְּכֹחַ נִתְּזוּ שָׁם הַמַּיִם, דָּאס הֵיְיסְט עֶס וֶועט אַרַיְין שְׁפְּרִיצֶען אֲפִלּוּ אִין דִּי כָּשֶׁרֶ'ה הֶערְצֶער (הַיְנוּ שֶׁיַּתִּיז גַּם בְּתוֹךְ הַלְּבָבוֹת הַכְּשֵׁרִים). וְעִם חָכְמוֹת לֹא יוּכְלוּ לִתֵּן עֵצָה, וְכָל שָׂרֵי הַמְּלוּכָה נִתְפַּזְּרוּ וְכָל הַמְּלוּכָה לֹא יִתְחַזֵּק עַל עָמְדוֹ, וֶועט זִיךְ נִיט דֶּער הַאלְטִין נָאר (לֹא יַחֲזִיקוּ מַעֲמָד רַק) פְּשׁוּטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאוֹמְרִים תְּהִלִּים בִּפְשִׁיטוּת וְכוּ'. עַל־כֵּן שֶׁכְּשֶׁיָּבוֹא מָשִׁיחַ
הֵם יִתְּנוּ הַכֶּתֶר מְלוּכָה בְּרֹאשׁוֹ.
* * * *
aligned_segments.en:
And similarly our master z"l pointed with his hands toward Moharan"as and R. Naftali z"l and said: "With them I rule countries — and with you I play chess." In sum — there is much to tell — and many sheets would not suffice to tell what he engaged with them etc.

And the end was: on the last Rosh HaShanah in Uman — the year 5571 [1810] — they prayed together in the gathering of our master z"l. And Hirsh Ber's maidservant came to call him to go drink coffee etc. He answered her: "Not this — that is: before the blowing of the shofar I am not going to drink." And he also began letting a small beard grow. And also Moharan"as z"l reviewed the Torah section 8 of Likutay Tinyono — "Tik'u" — together with Hirsh Ber mentioned above — for it was crowded in the house. And Moharan"as had only his ears turned toward our master z"l — while the rest of his body had the crush of people pressing against it. But Hirsh Ber was not pushed — for they feared him because of his closeness to the government etc. Therefore he heard the Torah well etc.

And after the passing of our master z"l — Moharan"as wept and lamented greatly as is known. They answered and said to him:

Aykh felt der Rebbe? Unz felt der Rebbe! Ven der Rebbe zol lebn, voltn mir gevorn baalei teshuvah un tzadikim gemurim! [You miss the Rebbe? We miss the Rebbe! If the Rebbe had lived — we would have become complete masters of repentance and complete Tzadikim!]

aligned_segments.he:
מָשָׁל מִוֶוערְדָא
מָשָׁל מִוֶוערְדָא, שֶׁסִּפֵּר רַבֵּנוּ זַ"ל שֶׁאִישׁ אֶחָד נָסַע עִם בַּעַל עֲגָלָה (לְבֶערְלִין אוֹ שְׁאָר עֲיָרוֹת הַגְּדוֹלוֹת), וְהָאִישׁ הָלַךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת צְרָכָיו, וְנִשְׁאַר הַבַּעַל עֲגָלָה שֶׁשְּׁמוֹ יִוַואן (הַמְגֻשָּׁם בְּלִי הֶרְגֵּשׁ) עִם הָעֲגָלָה בְּאֶמְצַע הַשּׁוּק. וְהָלַךְ אֵלָיו אִישׁ חַיִל (שׁוֹטֵר) וּשְׁאָלוֹ מַדּוּעַ עוֹמֵד שָׁם, וְאָמַר לוֹ וֶוערְדָא (מִי כָּאן). וְהוּא חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁשּׁוֹאֲלוֹ אֶת שְׁמוֹ וְאוֹמֵר לוֹ יִוַואן, וְהוּא מַכֶּה אוֹתוֹ וְאוֹמֵר וֶוערְדָא, וְהוּא צוֹעֵק יִוּוַאן, וְהוּא מַכֶּה אוֹתוֹ וְצוֹעֵק וֶוערְדָא עַד שֶׁלְּקָחוֹ עִם הָעֲגָלָה לְאֵיזֶה רְחוֹב מִן הַצַּד. וּכְשֶׁבָּא הָאִישׁ חִפְּשׂוֹ עַד שֶׁמְּצָאוֹ, וְאוֹמֵר לוֹ יִוַּואן וְכוּ', הוּא עוֹנֶה לוֹ בְּלַחַשׁ וּבְפַחַד אַל תֹּאמַר יִוַּואן אֶלָּא וֶוערְדָא, וְכֵיוָן שֶׁיָּצָא מֵהָעִיר הוּא אוֹמֵר לוֹ עַכְשָׁו אַתָּה יָכוֹל לִקְרֹא אוֹתִי יוַּואן. שָׁם נִקְרָא וֶוערְדָא וְשָׁם נִקְרָא יִוַּואן. וְסִיֵּם רַבֵּנוּ זַ"ל בַּא מִיר אִיז וֶוערְדָא (אֶצְלִי הוּא וֶוערְדָא) כְּלוֹמַר "מִי הוּא" שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ פְּחִיתוּתוֹ וְגַם נִזְדַּכֵּךְ הַגּוּף (הַיִּוַּואן) וְנִקְרָא בִּבְחִינַת מִי וּמַה וֶוערְדָא אִין מֶען גֵּיְיט אַרוֹיס פִין מִיר אִיז וִוידֶער יִוַּואן
(וּכְשֶׁיּוֹצְאִים מִמֶּנִי חוֹזֵר לִהְיוֹת יִוַואן). הַחֹמֶר הוּא חֹמֶר.
* * * *
aligned_segments.en:
And another story: after the passing of our master z"l — there were differences of opinion as to where to lay our master z"l to rest. For the Chevra Kadisha [burial society] did not wish to place our master z"l except in the new cemetery — since in the old one they had not placed anyone for a long time. And our fellowship from Teplyk specifically wanted to take our master z"l to Teplyk. And our fellowship from Tirhavitze wanted to take him to Tirhavitze. And only R. Nussun was the one who cried out that he knew our master z"l had specifically wished to rest in that old cemetery. And it is understood that R. Nussun was becoming uncertain — since he was only one. But immediately Hirsh Ber came to Moharan"as and asked him: if you know that the wish of our master z"l was to rest in the old cemetery — then wait a bit and complete your intentions. And he went immediately to the ispravnik [government official] and obtained a permit for two graves — therefore they were still able to make a small structure. [And for this structure — the second wife of our master z"l — who had no connection to him at all — said regarding him: "I would tell of your glory but have not seen you — I would liken you, name you — but have not known you" — roused herself that it be built with her money. And so it was. And the Rav R. Avrohom hinted regarding this: "His house — this is his wife."]

And after the passing of our master z"l — they were dear beloved friends to our fellowship — and especially to Moharan"as z"l. And Moharan"as z"l had a command from our master z"l to speak with them. Therefore every time he was in Uman he would pay them a visit and speak with them. And once he entered into such great philosophical investigations with them that he cried out and said: "What did our master z"l want of him?"

And also once there was one with our master z"l — and our master z"l asked him: "With what do you strengthen yourself in your fallen state from the service of Hashem?" He answered: with a page of Gemara. Our master z"l answered him: "I live in a great city and there are great heretics there — and I sustain myself with: 'Blessed is He who created us for His glory and separated us from those who err' etc." And some say this is one of the reasons [another version: the reason he traveled] that our master z"l chose Uman — in order to lift up R. Nussun and R. Naftali — whose hearts were very broken — and here, when they would see such heretics as these — they would sustain themselves that they are believers in Hashem etc.

And once Moharan"as came to them and they asked him a deep calculation — which a certain great wise priest had labored over for many years. He asked them to give him a private room — and he stayed there approximately an hour and a half — standing with one foot on the bench and the other on the floor — closing his eyes and deepening his mind — and he told them the answer. And they related how this priest labored for many years — and when he arrived at the answer he made a holiday and a feast. And Moharan"as z"l took this calculation and added to it some number — and told them that now — even if he would labor for many years — he would not arrive at it. And these heretics mentioned above — Moharan"as z"l was held in very great esteem among them — for they saw his righteousness and uprightness and his total devotion with all heart and soul to our master z"l. And this was very pleasing in their eyes.

aligned_segments.he:
מַעֲשֶׂה מִמָּרוֹר 
מַעֲשֶׂה מִמָּרוֹר שֶׁסִּפֵּר רַבֵּנוּ זַ"ל. שֶׁפַּעַם אַחַת הָלְכוּ יְהוּדִי וְגֶרְמָנִי יַחַד נְדוֹד, וְלִמֵּד הַיְּהוּדִי אֶת הַגֶּרְמָנִי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה אֶת עַצְמוֹ כְּמוֹ יְהוּדִי (כֵּיוָן שֶׁהַלָּשׁוֹן הוּא אֶחָד), וְהַיְּהוּדִים רַחֲמָנִים וִירַחֲמוּ עָלָיו. וְכֵיוָן שֶׁבָּא סָמוּךְ לְפֶסַח לִמְּדוֹ אֵיךְ שֶׁיִּתְנַהֵג (שֶׁיִּקְרָא אוֹתוֹ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת לַבַּיִת עַל הַסֵּדֶר) בְּכָל הַסֵּדֶר, שֶׁעוֹשִׂין קִדּוּשׁ, וְרוֹחֲצִים יָדַיִם, רַק שָׁכַח לֹאמַר לוֹ שֶׁאוֹכְלִים מָרוֹר. וְכֵיוָן שֶׁבָּא לְהַסֵּדֶר רָעֵב מִכָּל הַיּוֹם, וּמְצַפֶּה שֶׁיֹּאכַל הַדְּבָרִים טוֹבִים שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַיְּהוּדִי, אֲבָל נוֹתְנִים לוֹ חֲתִיכַת כַּרְפַּס בְּמֵי מֶלַח, וּשְׁאָר הַדְּבָרִים הַנּוֹהֲגִים בַּסֵּדֶר, וְאוֹמְרִים הַהַגָּדָה. וּכְבָר הוּא בְּעֵינַיִם צוֹפִיּוֹת לְהָאֲכִילָה, וְהוּא שָׂמֵחַ כְּבָר שֶׁאוֹכְלִים כְּבָר הַמַּצָּה. פִּתְאֹם נוֹתְנִים לוֹ מָרוֹר, וְנַעֲשָׂה לוֹ מַר בְּפִיו, וְהוּא חָשַׁב שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַסְּעֻדָּה שֶׁרַק זֶה יֹאכְלוּ. בָּרַח תֵּכֶף בִּמְרִירוּת וּרְעָבוֹן, וְחָשַׁב אֶל עַצְמוֹ יְהוּדִים אֲרוּרִים, אַחַר כָּל הַצֶּערְמָנְיָא (טֶקֶס) נוֹתְנִים זֶה לֶאֱכֹל. וּבָא לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ וְיָשֵׁן, וְאַחַר־כָּךְ בָּא הַיְּהוּדִי בְּפָנִים שְׂמֵחוֹת, שָׂבֵעַ מֵאֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה, וּשְׁאָלוֹ אֵיךְ הָיָה לְךָ הַסֵּדֶר, סִפֵּר לוֹ בְּכַעַס. אָמַר לוֹ הוֹי גֶּרְמָנִי שׁוֹטֶה, אִם הָיִיתָ מְחַכֶּה עוֹד מְעַט, הָיִיתָ
אוֹכֵל כָּל טוּב כָּמוֹנִי.
כֵּן הוּא בְּעִנְיַן רַבֵּנוּ (וַעֲבוֹדַת ה') שֶׁאַחַר כָּל הַיְגִיעוֹת וְהַטְּרָחוֹת עַד שֶׁבָּאִים, וְנִתְקָרְבִים לְרַבֵּנוּ אוֹ לַעֲבוֹדַת ה' לְזַכֵּךְ הַגּוּף נוֹתְנִים מְעַט מָרוֹר מְרִירוּת, כִּי זִכּוּךְ הַגּוּף בָּא בִּמְרִירוּת, אֲבָל הָאִישׁ חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁתָּמִיד יִהְיֶה רַק הַמְּרִירוּת, אַךְ זֶהוּ הַכֹּל רַק הַמְּרִירוּת וְכוּ' עַל־כֵּן בּוֹרֵחַ תֵּכֶף. אֲבָל כֵּיוָן שֶׁמְּחַכֶּה מְעַט וְסוֹבֵל זֶה הַמְּרִירוּת מְעַט מִזִּכּוּךְ הַגּוּף, אָז מַרְגִּישׁ אַחַר־כָּךְ כָּל מִינֵי חִיּוּת וְתַעֲנוּג (וְאֵלּוּ הַמְּשָׁלִים יְכוֹלִים לִלְמֹד מֵהֶם עֵצוֹת לְכָל עִנְיְנֵי עֲבוֹדַת ה'). כֵּן הוּא בְּעִנְיָן זֶה שֶׁל עֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם, שֶׁמִּקֹּדֶם עוֹבֵר הַמְּרִירוּת שֶׁל זִכּוּךְ הַגּוּף, אֲבָל אַחַר־כָּךְ
מַרְגִּישִׁים הַחִיּוּת וְכוּ'.
* * * *
aligned_segments.en:
And at the time of the great persecution against him — Hirsh Ber said to Moharan"as z"l: "If you agree — I will write a petition to the Emperor himself — and within twenty-four hours not a trace of the opponents will remain." And Moharan"as z"l answered him: "First — I do not wish G-d forbid that the opposition grow stronger. And second — I do not wish that they should be the persecuted and I the persecutor. I have no other counsel but prayer."

And once Hirsh Ber spoke with Moharan"as z"l about the existence of the Divine Being. He answered and said to him:

Vos redstu mit mir fun Got? Ikh zog dir: "Va'ere es Hashem" — ikh hob gezeen Got! [What are you speaking to me about G-d? I tell you: "And I saw Hashem" — I have seen G-d!]

And he believed him.

aligned_segments.he:
מעשה מהאוצר תחת הגשר
מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁסִּפֵּר מֵהָאוֹצָר שֶׁתַּחַת הַגֶּשֶׁר. שֶׁפַּעַם אַחַת חָלַם לְאִישׁ אֶחָד מֵאֵיזֶה עִיר שֶׁבְּוִינָה תַּחַת הַגֶּשֶׁר יֵשׁ שָׁם אוֹצָר, עַל־כֵּן נָסַע לְשָׁם וְעוֹמֵד אֵצֶל הַגֶּשֶׁר וּמְחַפֵּשׂ עֵצוֹת אֵיךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת, כִּי בַּיּוֹם אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל מֵחֲמַת הָאֲנָשִׁים, וְעָבַר שָׁם אִישׁ חַיִל וְאָמַר לוֹ מָה אַתָּה עוֹמֵד וְחוֹשֵׁב. חָשַׁב בְּדַעְתּוֹ שֶׁטּוֹב שֶׁיֹּאמַר לוֹ כְּדֵי שֶׁהוּא יְסַיְּעוֹ וְיִתְחַלְּקוּ, וְסִפֵּר לוֹ כָּל הָעִנְיָן. עָנָה וְאָמַר לוֹ אַיי יְהוּדִי נָאר קוּקְט אוֹיף אַ חֲלוֹם, אֶלָּא מַאי מִיר הָאט זִיךְ אוֹיְךְ גִּיחוּלֶמְתְּ אָז דָּא אִין דָּא בַּא דֶּעם אִין דֶּעם (וְהִזְכִּיר הָעִיר שֶׁל הָאִישׁ וּשְׁמוֹ שֶׁל הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה) אִין מַאקְזָאן אִיז דָּא אֵיין אוֹצָר וֶועל אִיךְ פָארִין צִיא יֶענוּם? וְנָסַע הָאִישׁ לְבֵיתוֹ וְחָפַר בְּהַמַקְאזַאן שֶׁלּוֹ וּמָצָא הָאוֹצָר. וְאָמַר אַחַר־כָּךְ אִיצְט וֵויְיס אִיךְ שׁוֹין "דֶּער אוֹצָר אִיז בַּא מִיר, נָאר וִויסֶען פוּם דֶּעם אוֹצָר מוּז מֶען פָארִין קֵיין וִוין" (הוֹי יְהוּדִי שָׂם לֵב לַחֲלוֹם אֱלָא מַאי גַּם אֲנִי חָלַמְתִּי שֶׁבְּמָקוֹם פְּלוֹנִי אֵצֶל פְּלוֹנִי בַּמַּחְסָן יֵשׁ אוֹצָר, הַאֶסַע לְשָׁם. וְנָסַע הָאִישׁ לְבֵיתוֹ וְחָפַר בַּמַּחְסָן שֶׁלּוֹ וּמָצָא הָאוֹצָר. וְאָמַר אַחַר־כָּךְ, "עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי: הָאוֹצָר הוּא אֶצְלִי אֲבָל כְּדֵי לָדַעַת מִזֶּה עָלַי לִנְסֹעַ עַד וִינָה"). כָּךְ בְּעִנְיַן עֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם, שֶׁהָאוֹצָר הוּא אֵצֶל כָּל אֶחָד בְּעַצְמוֹ, רַק לֵידַע מֵהָאוֹצָר מֻכְרָח לִסַּע
לְהַצַּדִּיק.
* * * *
aligned_segments.en:
Once when Landa came from Berdichev he brought many gifts to his house etc. — and immediately when he heard that Moharan"as z"l was in Uman — before going home he went to him. And Moharan"as z"l spoke with them of the ultimate purpose — that this world is nothing etc. — and the world is full of sorrows etc. And it was a wonder in their minds — for they thought: I have just come from Berdichev and I have all good things etc. He answered and said: "A person can come from Berdichev with many gifts — and bring his wife a golden ring — and it may not please her — and a quarrel will ensue until he wishes death better than life." And so it was immediately with Landa — that he went home and gave his wife the golden ring — and it did not please her — and a quarrel ensued — until literally death was better than life for him. And he went immediately to Moharan"as z"l and said:

Oy, hot ihr gut tsugetrofn! [Oy — you guessed exactly right!]

And at the time of the persecution against Moharan"as z"l — they gave him strengthening not to become downhearted. And they told him a story that once happened in the world: a doctor had a student-assistant. And as time went on — the masses began to make much of the assistant more than the doctor — until he became famous in the world and more honored. And once the king made a banquet — and everyone sat according to their honor. And the student-assistant sat first and afterwards the doctor. The doctor answered and said to the assistant:

Du veyst dokh yo dem khiluk fun mir biz dir. [You know well the difference between me and you.]

aligned_segments.he:
משל מהינדיק
הַמָּשָׁל מֵהָהִינְדִיק (תַּרְנְגוֹל הֹדּוּ). שֶׁפַּעַם אַחַת בֶּן הַמֶּלֶךְ נָפַל לְשִׁגָּעוֹן שֶׁהוּא עוֹף הַנִּקְרָא הִינְדִיק, וְצָרִיךְ לֵישֵׁב עָרֹם תַּחַת הַשֻּׁלְחָן וְלִגְרֹר חֲתִיכוֹת לֶחֶם וַעֲצָמוֹת כְּמוֹ הִינְדִיק. וְכָל הָרוֹפְאִים נוֹאֲשׁוּ מִלַּעֲזֹר לוֹ וּלְרַפְּאוֹתוֹ מִזֶּה, וְהַמֶּלֶךְ הָיָה בְּצַעַר גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה. עַד שֶׁבָּא חָכָם אֶחָד וְאָמַר אֲנִי מְקַבֵּל עַל עַצְמִי לְרַפְּאוֹתוֹ, וְהִפְשִׁיט גַּם־כֵּן אֶת עַצְמוֹ עָרֹם וַיֵּשֶׁב תַּחַת הַשֻּׁלְחָן אֵצֶל בֶּן הַמֶּלֶךְ הַנַּ"ל, וְגַם־כֵּן גָּרַר פֵּרוּרִים וַעֲצָמוֹת. וּשְׁאָלוֹ בֶּן הַמֶּלֶךְ מִי אַתָּה וּמָה אַתָּה עוֹשֶׂה פֹּה?, וְהֵשִׁיב לוֹ וּמָה אַתָּה עוֹשֶׂה פֹּה?, אָמַר לוֹ אֲנִי הִינְדִיק, אָמַר לוֹ אֲנִי גַּם־כֵּן הִינְדִיק. וַיֵּשְׁבוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם יַחַד כָּךְ אֵיזֶה זְמַן עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ רְגִילִים זֶה עִם זֶה. וְאָז רָמַז הֶחָכָם וְהִשְׁלִיכוּ לָהֶם כְּתֹנֶת, וְאָמַר הֶחָכָם הָהִינְדִיק לְהַבֶּן מֶלֶךְ אַתָּה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁהִינְדִיק אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לֵילֵךְ עִם כְּתֹנֶת, יְכוֹלִים לִהְיוֹת לָבוּשׁ כְּתֹנֶת וְאַף־עַל־ פִּי־כֵן יְהֵא הִינְדִיק, וְלָבְשׁוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם הַכְּתֹנֶת. וְאַחַר אֵיזֶה זְמַן רָמַז וְהִשְׁלִיכוּ לָהֶם מִכְנָסַיִם. וְאָמַר לוֹ גַּם־כֵּן כַּנַּ"ל, אַתָּה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁעִם מִכְנָסַיִם לֹא יְכוֹלִים לִהְיוֹת הִינְדִיק וְכוּ' עַד שֶׁלָּבְשׁוּ הַמִכְנָסַיִם וְכֵן עִם שְׁאָר הַבְּגָדִים. וְאַחַר־כָּךְ רָמַז וְהִשְׁלִיכוּ לָהֶם מַאַכְלֵי אָדָם מֵהַשֻּׁלְחָן וְאָמַר לוֹ, אַתָּה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁאִם אוֹכְלִים מַאֲכָלִים טוֹבִים אוּז מֶען שׁוֹין קֵיין הִינְדִיק נִיט, מֶען קֶען עֶסִין אוּן אוֹיְךְ זַיין הִינְדִיק (כְּבָר לֹא נִקְרָאִים הִינְדִיק, אֶפְשַׁר לֶאֱכֹל וּלְהַמְשִׁיךְ לִהְיוֹת הִינְדִיק) וְאָכְלוּ. וְאַחַר־כָּךְ אָמַר לוֹ אַתָּה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁהִינְדִיק מֻכְרָח לִהְיוֹת דַּוְקָא תַּחַת הַשֻּׁלְחָן, יְכוֹלִים לִהְיוֹת הִינְדִיק וְלִהְיוֹת אֵצֶל הַשֻּׁלְחָן. וְכֵן הִתְנַהֵג עִמּוֹ עַד שֶׁרִפֵּא אוֹתוֹ לְגַמְרֵי. וְהַנִּמְשָׁל מוּבָן לַמְּבִינִים.
aligned_segments.en:
He answered him: "Do not be downhearted — do not lose heart — for such is the way of the world in every generation: ninety-eight percent do not know from the truth — and two percent know. And so too with Moharan"as z"l."

And after the passing of Moharan"as z"l — Hirsh Ber traveled to America — and was writing letters of friendship to R. Nachman of Tulchin z"l. And when he passed away there — his sons wrote to R. Nachman mentioned above at length about his passing — and that he passed away in repentance — and his mouth never ceased saying:

Oy der Rebbe, oy der Rebbe! [Oy — the Rebbe! Oy — the Rebbe!]

Once on Erev Shabbos — as our master z"l was traveling to Breslov and the day was still long — he said to his men: "I think that when we come to Breslov — it will be after the bathhouse" —

— and so it was — that when they came to Breslov — the bathhouse had burned down that day.

Regarding the evil eye [ ayin hora ] spoken of in the conversations: the attendant complained before him z"l that he asked a certain man to give him one horse from his two horses — and he would not. Our master z"l said to him: "If so — he has only one horse." He requested the calf — and our master z"l said: "If so — he has no calf." When the attendant returned to that man — he found that one horse had died and only one remained — and the calf had also died.

הַמָּשָׁל מֵהַתְּבוּאָה. שֶׁפַּעַם אַחַת אָמַר הַמֶּלֶךְ לַאֲהוּבוֹ הַשֵּׁנִי לַמֶּלֶךְ בַּאֲשֶׁר אֲנִי חוֹזֶה בַּכּוֹכָבִים, רוֹאֶה אֲנִי שֶׁכָּל הַתְּבוּאָה שֶׁיִּגְדַּל בְּשָׁנָה זֹאת, מִי שֶׁיֹּאכַל מִמֶּנָּה יִהְיֶה נַעֲשֶׂה מְשֻׁגָּע, אִם כֵּן יְטַכֵּס עֵצָה. וְעָנָה לוֹ, שֶׁעַל־כֵּן יָכִינוּ בַּעֲדָם תְּבוּאָה שֶׁלֹּא יִצְטָרְכוּ לֶאֱכֹל מִתְּבוּאָה הַנַּ"ל. וְעָנָה לוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ אִם־כֵּן כְּשֶׁאֲנַחְנוּ לְבַד לֹא נִהְיֶה מְשֻׁגָּעִים, וְכָל הָעוֹלָם יִהְיֶה מְשֻׁגָּע, אָז יִהְיֶה לְהֵפֶךְ שֶׁאֲנַחְנוּ יִהְיוּ הַמְשֻׁגָּעִים, (וּלְהָכִין בִּשְׁבִיל כֻּלָּם אִי אֶפְשָׁר), עַל־כֵּן בְּוַדַּאי נִצְטָרֵךְ גַּם־כֵּן לֶאֱכֹל מֵהַתְּבוּאָה, אֲבָל רַק זֶה שֶׁנְּסַמֵּן סִימָן עַל מִצְחֵנוּ שֶׁנֵּדַע עַל־כָּל־פָּנִים שֶׁאֲנַחְנוּ מְשֻׁגָּע. שֶׁאִם אֶהְיֶה מִסְתַּכֵּל עַל מִצְחֲךָ

Moshe Hinkes related that once early in the morning when he went to the mikveh and the way passed by the house of our master z"l — he attempted to peer into our master's z"l house through the cracks in the shutters to see what our master z"l was doing. And he saw our master z"l from behind — his face to the wall. At noon he was again with our master z"l — and suddenly our master z"l told him that one must seal and plaster the cracks — for the sight through one crack —

eyn kuk fun ashpering iz mikh oykh mevalbel — gam ken mevalbel osi [one glance through a crack disturbs me too — it also disturbs me]

Once a man and woman came to our master z"l requesting that he pray for them regarding children. Our master z"l said to them in this language:

Ihr vet ba mir gehalfen vern tsvishn tog un nakht [You will be helped by me between day and night]

הַמָּשָׁל מִמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁרָץ אַחַר צְבִי וְלֹא יָכֹל לְהַשִּׂיגוֹ, וְהֶעֱמִידוּ אֶת עַצְמָם הַשָּׂרֵי מְלוּכָה וְאָמְרוּ אֲדוֹנֵנוּ הַמֶּלֶךְ נַחֲזֹר וְכוּ', עָנָה הַמֶּלֶךְ וְאָמַר אֲנִי אֶת הַצְּבִי מֻכְרָח לָצוּד וּמִי שֶׁרוֹצֶה לַחֲזֹר

aligned_segments.en:
And this man lived in a village near Uman. And once after the passing of our master z"l — the man and his wife came to Uman for the mitzvah of immersion. And when they left — it was twilight [between day and night]. And they went by way of the holy grave and prayed there with streaming tears. And they returned from there and traveled home — and that year they were blessed with a male son and named him Nachman after our master z"l. After time — when their son Nachman grew up — at that time the decree of military conscription went out upon the world. And this young man Nachman was also required to appear for the medical review. And when his time to appear came — he first went to the holy grave of our master z"l and wept there greatly. And when his father and mother came to him — he told them that he had dreamed: there came to him a young married man whose appearance was thus and thus [and they recognized this was the appearance of our master z"l] — and said to him: "Were you not named after me? — You shall not serve among them." And a miracle occurred — leprosy broke out on his body — and from this he was freed from military service. And after a short time he was healed and became healthy as before.

A story of one who suddenly fell ill at night — and the relatives of the sick man came to our master z"l. And our master z"l began to put them off a bit — and they began to insist. Our master z"l said to them: "Bring me two hundred silver rubles — with every kind of coin." And they began to search for money — and it was presumably hard to find at night. And much time passed until they had found the money — but they found coins. And one coin of five rubles they searched for — until the sick man died, G-d have mercy. And then it became day. And then they found the five silver rubles in the pocket of the sick man himself.

Once one of our fellowship [he was R. Tevye the grocer of Tirhavitze] came to our master z"l — and our master z"l spoke with him: that it is certainly better for a person to be poor, G-d forbid, than to die, G-d forbid. [For when the money is taken from the person — certainly it is better than when the person is taken from the money etc.] For when a person is alive — Hashem can give him all good etc. And the man agreed with our master z"l. And our master z"l concluded then: "Even Nachman Nussun would have been pleased to be poor rather than to lie under a clod of earth." And the man traveled home — and on the way he heard that his house and possessions had burned — and the souls had escaped. And he also heard that Nachman Nussun was traveling from Petersburg with a sack full of gold coins — and suddenly he became ill — and could not make it to the city in time — and perished on the road and was buried there, G-d have mercy — for he had already become greatly decomposed etc. And then the man saw the holy spirit of our master z"l.

When R. Nussun z"l heard from our master z"l that it is good for each person to have a private room for hisbodedus and for all particulars of the service of Hashem — he began to yearn for this. And it occurred to him to build himself an upper room etc. — as it is also brought in the Book of Traits that to dwell in an upper story is good for the service of the Creator. But from the immensity of his poverty — he thought for a long time how long he would need to spend gathering money and building a structure. And he said in this language:

Vifil Torah un tefilah ikh darf tsu lib dem onverin! [How much Torah and prayer would I need to lose for this!]

Therefore for now he found a solution to make do — by making himself a partition in the room he lived in — fully enclosed. And in those four cubits he merited to compose the entire book of prayers that he left after him as a blessing. And in time he merited an upper room — some years before his passing z"tl.

What is mentioned in the letters of Moharan"as regarding the necessity of strengthening oneself — and without it the danger is great — and the proof from the rabbi of Balfur etc. — this was the story: there was a rabbi — a Gaon — great in Torah and wisdom — and he was a righteous man. And because he lacked strengthening at the time of his falling — this caused him in the end to fall completely from Judaism, G-d have mercy.

The story of Moharan"as in which was fulfilled regarding him "I will give a man in your place" — that it was decreed upon him etc. — and that night there fell upon a certain proper man named R. Nussun the pharmacist [see the letters of Moharan"as ] — and they killed him and all his household. And that night the shammes [beadle] at the cemetery heard a great noise from the grave of his [R. Nussun pharmacist's] father — and in the morning when he heard that his son R. Nussun had been killed — they understood that this was the noise: that he had wished to rescue him and was unable. And this had been decreed upon Moharan"as z"l — and was exchanged for that man — whose name was Nussun.

Our master z"l said to R. Lippa: "Look at me" —

Kuk mikh on

— "And what I do not say to them [he pointed with his hand toward R. Nussun and R. Naftali z"l] — for they see me every time." And further he said: "You see me now — you will see me on Rosh HaShanah." He explicitly said that the study of his compositions is the beginning of the redemption — speedily in our days, Amen.

Further I found written in a volume that was with R. Naftali z"l:

נִמְצָא בִּמְגִלַּת סְתָרִים זֶה הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, מֵעִנְיַן סֵפֶר אֵלִים. וְהוּא סֵפֶר יָקָר מְאֹד שֶׁחִבְּרוֹ אִישׁ אֱלֹקִים רַבִּי יוֹסֵף קַאנְדִיָּא זַ"ל.

a) "I will seek him in whatever place he is — like the court [Beis Din]." b) What the world is accustomed to doing for the evil eye — to spit toward it — is hinted in the words of our Sages z"l regarding Chananya Mishael and Azarya: where did they go? One said: they died from the evil eye. And one said: they were drowned in spittle. That is — the hint mentioned: that they feared the evil eye — and he spat toward them — and they died from the spit. c) He has a heavenly constellation [ma'arachah] — and this alone will be his downfall. d) He boasts in winter — for he defied the battle-arrays of the living G-d. But David was not afraid of him at all — and said that he had already had an encounter with seven — and he had grasped him by his beard. For the lion came etc. "and I grasped his beard" — he grasped him by the beard and struck and killed him — so shall it be. (Said the transcriber: He saw he has a battle-array. Until here these were said regarding the matter etc. that was related before him etc. — that there would be a strong winter.) These stories were written in the volume mentioned that was with R. Naftali: "The story of a small king who was conquered by a great king — as printed in the New Story-books."

— Stories and Parables of Rebbe Nachman of Breslov —From the gold-standard translation

Story 1 Mazal — Fortune and the Thief A story of a pauper who would sit in the study house [Beis Medrash] and study Torah. Once an astrologer [called rosh bit — a stargazer] came to the city — and the whole city ran to him. But the pauper sat in the study house and did not go. His wife came to him inside the study house — and found no one there except her husband — for all had gone to the seer. And she screamed at him: "You destitute lazy mishap! Why do you not go to the astrologer?" He did not want to go — and she badgered him further — until he was forced to go. He came to the astrologer — and the astrologer told him that his mazal [fate, fortune, aptitude] was that he should be a thief. He returned to the study house to his learning — and his wife came and said to him: "What did he tell you?" He said to her: "He said to me: 'A beggar — remain a beggar.'" In the evening he came home and ate his main meal — namely a piece of bread. While eating he began to chuckle — and his wife asked him: "What are you laughing about? Certainly you know something and you do not want to tell me." He said to her: "No — he told me nothing — I am simply laughing." He ate more — and again a second time he began to laugh — and she asked as before and he answered as before. In the middle of all this he burst out laughing — and laughed so heartily he emitted an odor from his mouth. She said to him again: "See — certainly you know something." He told her: the astrologer had told him his mazal was to be a thief. She replied: she did not want him to be a thief — "and it is good for us to be poor however it may be as Hashem provides — and you shall not be a thief." Afterwards Shabbos arrived — presumably they had everything nice for Shabbos in proper order — that is, challah loaves of grain bread and the rest of the courses duly [though this appears somewhat ironic]. And they sat to eat — and he had presumably four or five daughters and they grabbed from each other a piece of bread — for even the aforementioned bread he did not have adequate sufficiency. His wife spoke up and said: "Master of the World! I am already very fed up with this poverty to the extent that I want you to be a thief — so that we do not suffer this scrimping." He was forced to fulfill her desire: Ya givalt un nit givalt — in fort gegangen. [He did want and/or he did not want — nevertheless he went.] — and so each time Rebbe Nachman used this expression. He went to steal — and settled upon going to the wealthiest man of the city. He went to steal — and found the guards sleeping — and no one challenged him whatsoever. He went to the store — and the lock was open — for such was his mazal. And he went to the register — and its lock was open as well. He took four or five rubles — just enough for his livelihood — and brought them to his wife and said: "See — I have fulfilled your desire — draw your expenses from this — for I will not continue to steal again." She answered: certainly she also did not desire this — only she was compelled by the dire straits. Afterwards once she began screaming at him again: "Beggar-mishap — you were in the store — why did you not take enough for me a yoopa [a long unlined silk robe worn for formal occasions]?" And he was forced to go steal again. He went to the store and found a thief standing there — and asked him: "Who are you?" And he replied: "I am a thief." And so the other asked him — and he answered likewise that he is a thief. The pauper said to him: "Let us become partners in robberies — I have the mazal for this." And he agreed. The pauper said in his mind: if we steal here we will make the owner of the house a pauper — for I by myself would steal just what I need for a yoopa. But now he will steal a great deal and the owner will be left with nothing. So he said to the thief: "Why should we bring loss to a Jew — better that we go steal from a gentile." And he agreed — and they decided to go steal from the king [who lived in this city] — for certainly he could steal there — for that was his mazal. The thief said: "It would be good for us to steal the king's set of coronation clothing — and certainly it will be enough for us for generations upon generations — for I know where they are placed." The pauper agreed — for certainly he could steal them — for that was his mazal. And they went there — went through room after room — and found the clothing. And the pockets of the clothing were very valuable — and they took them. Afterwards they began to quarrel between them — because one garment was large and one was small. The thief said he was entitled to the large one because he had the intelligence about them. And the pauper said he was entitled to the large one because he was the one with the mazal — and with his mazal they stole them. The pauper said: "I will go ask the king." The thief said: "How is that possible?" He said: "Nevertheless — I will go ask him." The thief said: "If you could do this — that you go and ask the king — then I myself will give you the large garment." He went with him to the king — and lying near the king was one who told stories to the king so that he would sleep. So they came — and both grasped the king's bed where he was sleeping — and carried the bed with the king to another room. In the interim the king woke up and thought he was in his usual place. And the thief began to tell him the story as above — of the two thieves — and asked the king: "Who is entitled to the large garment?" The king was outraged: "What are you asking me? Certainly the pauper is entitled — because they were stolen with his mazal! It would be good for you to tell me a story." And he told him a story — and the king slept. They stood and carried the bed back and returned it to the first room. In the morning it became known that the king's coronation clothing had been stolen. The king remembered that the one who lay by him had told him the aforementioned story and asked him who was entitled to the large garment — and he realized he must know from the robbery. So they beat him — and he said he did not know — and they beat him profusely and tortured him greatly — but he maintained: "I do not know." The king sent for the archbishop [called archiriga] to ask about the story — whether it was possible that the man still had not stolen them. The priest said it was possible he did not know. And the priest said it was foolish of the king to have ruled that the pauper was entitled to the large garment. The king was greatly outraged at the priest for considering him a fool — and wished to do something to him but was unable. And they searched greatly for the theft but did not find anything. The king commanded to announce: whoever had stolen should come and acknowledge it — for certainly nothing would be done to him — as the king desired to know how it was possible to steal these garments. And crowds of people congregated discussing this. The pauper came and asked them: "What are you discussing?" And they informed him. He spoke up and said: "What is the commotion? He who stole will return." And they screamed at him. And so he came again and asked — and they screamed at him: "Beggar — behold you are liable for your life — for they will say you know about the theft." He said: "Yes — I know of the theft." They said: "If you know — go and tell." He said: "I will tell." So the pauper came to the king and said: "I know of the theft." The king said he greatly desired to see the thief. He replied: "I am he." And the king kissed him — and asked: "How did you steal them?" And he told him the whole story — and they sought the thief and returned also the second garment which was by him. The king said to the pauper: "Devise contrivances to ensnare the aforementioned archbishop — for I am upset with him." He said: "So I will do." The pauper commanded to make for him clothing like the archbishop wears when conducting their prayers — and to catch many fish-reptiles [called rukes] — and to give him many candles. And he went and dressed himself in the clothing — and affixed a candle to each reptile — and lit the candles — and let the reptiles run and fly inside the priest's prayer house. And he stood at the place from which things are conducted. And he began to shout — and all gathered there. And the priest also came — and was very frightened — for he saw a flame and a voice calling but did not know what it was. He [the pauper] said to the priest that he had revealed himself to him — for he wished to bring him immediately to paradise. The priest fell on his face — and the pauper said to him that before he could enter paradise he must first go a bit to hell — and afterwards he would bring him to paradise. And he commanded the priest to get into a sack — and he got in. He went and tied him and carried him to the king — and hung him before the king's courtyard and informed him. Everyone went out and saw someone hanging in a sack — and did not know what it was — and began throwing stones at it — and threw so many stones until they hit him beaten and bruised and broke all his teeth. And the priest did not know what this was — if this was the hell he was told about — that he must go to first — or if this was a trick. Afterwards when they had beaten him — the king said to throw him out — and they threw him out and untied the sack — and he left there in great disgrace. [In an alternate version heard: the end was that they took him to be hanged — for the end of a thief is to be hanged. And when they were bringing him — someone [the Accuser] went with a sack of shoes and said to him: "So much effort I toiled — and so many shoes I wore out — until I brought you to this etc."] (The transcriber says: for this is the way of the Accuser — to entice and afterwards to goad, as is brought in Story Tale #8 about the rabbi and his only son etc.) In Siach Sarfey Kodesh (3:99) the alternate version is: when the pauper is told that the king desires to see the thief — "He did want and/or he did not want" — and yet he goes and tells the king the whole story from beginning to end. The royal ministers and judges tell the king: even though you do not hold it against him and pardon him — we demand justice. And they decreed that his punishment was to be hanged. When they were taking him to be hanged — he saw from afar the astrologer carrying a sack full of torn shoes etc.

בְּיָמָיו נִתְקַבְּצוּ חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת תַּלְמִידִים מֻפְלְגֵי תּוֹרָה, וְהִתְחִילוּ לִלְמֹד בְּסִפְרֵי חֲקִירָה וּבְמוֹרֶה נְבוֹכִים עַד שֶׁנִּתְפַּקְּרוּ וְכָפְרוּ בֵּאלֹקִים חַיִּים וְאָמְרוּ שֶׁהָעוֹלָם וְכוּ' וְאֵין הַשְׁגָּחַת אֱלֹקִים עַל הָעוֹלָם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם. וַיָּבֹאוּ כָּל הַתַּלְמִידִים הַנַּ"ל לְהַצַּדִּיק רַבִּי יוֹסֵף קַאנְדִיָּא זַ"ל שֶׁגַּם הוּא יַסְכִּים עִמָּהֶם עַל הַדָּבָר הָרָע הַזֶּה. וְהַצַּדִּיק הַנַּ"ל כְּשֶׁשָּׁמַע הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה אֲחָזַתּוּ פַּלָּצוּת. וְהִתְחִילוּ לְהַרְאוֹת רְאָיוֹת וּלְהִתְוַכֵּחַ עִמּוֹ, וְלֹא הָיָה יָכוֹל לַהֲשִׁיבָם מִדָּבָר הַזֶּה. וַיַּעַן וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם תְּנוּ לִי
אֵיזֶה זְמַן וְאָשִׁיב אֶתְכֶם. וַיִּתְּנוּ לוֹ אֵיזֶה זְמַן וְהָלְכוּ לָהֶם.
וְהַצַּדִּיק הַנַּ"ל שָׁלַח אִגְּרוֹת לְכָל הָרַבָּנִים הַגְּדוֹלִים שֶׁיָּבֹאוּ אֵלָיו מְהֵרָה. וַיָּבוֹאוּ אֵלָיו. וַיְסַפֵּר לָהֶם הַדָּבָר הַנַּ"ל, וַיִּתְפַּלְּלוּ כֻּלָּם אֶל ה' וַיָּצוּמוּ לַיְלָה וָיוֹם, וְגַם הַצַּדִּיק הַנַּ"ל נָפַל עַל פָּנָיו אַרְצָה שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים וְשָׁלֹשׁ לֵילוֹת לֶחֶם לֹא אָכַל וּמַיִם לֹא שָׁתָה. אַחַר הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים וַיָּקָם מְהֵרָה מֵעַל הָאָרֶץ, וַיֹּאמֶר: "עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת לַה' הֵפֵרוּ תּוֹרָתֶךָ", וַיִּקַּח עֵט סוֹפֵר בְּיָדוֹ וַיִּכְתֹּב בְּלִי מַרְגּוֹעַ לֹא אָכַל וְלֹא שָׁתָה לֹא לָמַד וְלֹא הִתְפַּלֵּל רַק כָּתַב בְּעֵט סוֹפֵר, וַיְחַבֵּר אֶת הַסֵּפֶר הַנַּ"ל הַנִּקְרָא סֵפֶר אֵלִים, וְאַחַר־כָּךְ כְּשֶׁבָּאוּ כָּל הַתַּלְמִידִים וַיִּקַּח אֶת הַסֵּפֶר הַנַּ"ל וַיִּתֵּן בְּיָדָם. וְעִם הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה נִצֵחַ אוֹתָם, כִּי שָׁם יֵשׁ כָּל הַחָכְמוֹת וְרָאוּ חָכְמָתוֹ וְאַף־עַל־פִּי־כֵן מַאֲמִין כֵּן נִרְאֶה לִי.
וְנַעֲשׂוּ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים.

Story 2 One Thing Brought the Success What is brought in the Words of Rabbi Nachman [Sichos HaRan] (item 166): that he said — "With one thing I was successful — and through this I merited to what I merited" — and he said it in this language: Mit ayn zakh iz mir gerotin. And it is not explained there what the thing is. And I heard that he said: for it is brought in the words of the kabbalists that Adam HuRishon [the first man] — when he ate from the Tree of Knowledge — all the souls tasted. But his [Na Nach Nachma Nachman MeUman's] holy soul merited that it did not taste from the Tree of Knowledge whatsoever.

* * * *

Story 3 A Man Stronger Than a Diamond A story that Rebbe Nachman told over. A story of a pauper who supported himself from digging clay to sell. Once he was digging clay — and found in the place that he dug a gem which was worth an absolute fortune — but he did not know its value. So he went to an appraiser who answered that there was no one in this country who could pay its value — and he would need to travel to London, to the imperial city. But he was poor and had no money to travel. So he went and sold everything he had — and went from house to house for donations — until he had enough to travel to the sea. And he wanted to board the ship but had no money. So he went to the captain and showed him the gem — and immediately the captain took him aboard the ship with great honor and said to him: "You are a great certainty." And he gave him a special first-class cabin with all the amenities like a prized magnate. And his cabin had a window into the sea. And he was always delighting and rejoicing his soul with the diamond — and especially at mealtimes — for through joy and an expanded heart it is beneficial and healing — facilitating the digestion of food. One time he sat to eat — and the diamond was resting on the table to be delighted with — and he fell asleep. In the interim the servant came and took the tablecloth and the crumbs — and not knowing about the diamond — threw everything into the sea. And when he awoke from his sleep and understood all this — he had great anguish and almost went out of his mind. And what could he do? The captain is a marauder who would kill him for the price of the trip. Therefore he made himself happy as if he did not know. And the custom of the captain was to speak with him every day for a few hours — and so he came on this day. And he made himself happy to such an extent that the captain recognized no change in him. And the captain said to him: "I know you are wise and of straight heart — and I want to buy a great deal of grain to sell in London — and I can profit handsomely — but I am worried that they should not say I steal from the king's treasury. Therefore the purchase will be in your name — and I will pay you well." This was appealing in his eyes — and they did so. Immediately upon their arrival in London — the captain died — and everything was left with this man — and it was double and quadruple the value of the diamond. And Rebbe Nachman concluded: the diamond was not his — and the proof is that it was lost from him. And the grain was his — and the proof is that it remained with him. Un vus ehr iz gekumen tzu zayn zakh iz nur viel ehr hut zich dehr halten — [And everything that came to his cause was only due to his holding himself up etc.]

הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל הָיָה רַב בְּאֵיזֶה קְהִלָּה וְהָיָה יוֹשֵׁב וְלוֹמֵד עִם הַיְשִׁיבָה שֶׁלּוֹ כָּל הַיּוֹם כֻּלּוֹ. וְהָיָה אָז רַב דִּמְדִינָה בְּאוֹתוֹ הָאִיקְלִים (אֵזוֹר) שֶׁהָיָה הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל תַּחַת מֶמְשֶׁלֶת אוֹתוֹ הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה, וְהָיוּ מֻכְרָחִים כָּל הָרַבָּנִים שֶׁל הַקְּהִלּוֹת שֶׁשַּׁיָּכִים לְהָרַב דִּמְדִינָה לָבוֹא לִפְנֵי הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה לְקַבֵּל פָּנָיו וְלִטֹּל מִמֶּנּוּ רְשׁוּת, כַּנָּהוּג בַּדּוֹרוֹת שֶׁלְּפָנֵינוּ. וְכֵן הָיָה, שֶׁבָּאוּ כָּל הָרַבָּנִים כֻּלָּם שֶׁל כָּל הַקְּהִלּוֹת לְהָרַב דִּמְדִינָה לְקַבֵּל פָּנָיו. וְהָרַב הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל לֹא בָּא אֵלָיו רַק הָיָה יוֹשֵׁב וְלוֹמֵד תָּמִיד. וְדָן אוֹתוֹ הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה לְכַף זְכוּת וְאָמַר, אוּלַי מֵחֲמַת שֶׁטָּרוּד בְּגִרְסָה עַל כֵּן לֹא בָּא אֶל שֻׁלְחַן הַמֶּלֶךְ. וְנִתְיַשֵּׁב הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה וְנָסַע אֶצְלוֹ אֶל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר הָיָה חוֹנֶה שָׁם הָרַב הַקָּדוֹשׁ הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל, וּבָא אֶל הָעִיר וַיֶּחֶרְדוּ כָּל הָעִיר לִקְרָאתוֹ כַּנָּהוּג, וּבָאוּ כֻּלָּם לְקַבֵּל פָּנָיו, וְהָרַב הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל לֹא אָבָה לָלֶכֶת אֵלָיו. וְדָנוֹ הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה גַּם־כֵּן לְכַף זְכוּת, וְתָלָה גַּם זֹאת בְּבִטּוּל תּוֹרָה שֶׁאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לְבַטֵּל מִלִּמּוּדוֹ. וְאָמַר הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה אֲנִי אֵלֵךְ אֵלָיו, וְעָמַד הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה וְהָלַךְ אֶל בֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת שֶׁהָיָה יוֹשֵׁב שָׁם הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל עִם תַּלְמִידָיו, וּבָא אֶל הַבֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת. וְהָרַב הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א לֹא זָז מִמְּקוֹמוֹ וְלֹא הִפְסִיק מִלִּמּוּדוֹ, וְלֹא נָתַן לוֹ שָׁלוֹם כְּלָל. אַף־עַל־פִּי־כֵן דָּנוֹ לְכַף זְכוּת גַּם עַכְשָׁו, וְאָמַר אוּלַי גַּם זֶה מֵחֲמַת שֶׁאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לִפְסֹק
פּוּמֵהּ מִגִּרְסָה.
בְּתוֹךְ כָּךְ בָּא בָּחוּר אֶחָד יְפֵה עֵינַיִם לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת, וּמִיָּד חָרַד הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א לִקְרָאתוֹ וְקָם מִלְּפָנָיו מְלֹא קוֹמָתוֹ וְחָלַק לוֹ כָּבוֹד, וְדִבֵּר עִמּוֹ הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד. אָז קָצַף הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה מְאֹד עַל הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל וְכָעַס עָלָיו מְאֹד וּבִזָּה אוֹתוֹ, וְאָמַר, בִּתְחִלָּה כְּשֶׁלֹּא בָּאתֶם אֵלַי לִמְקוֹמִי דַּנְתִּי אֶתְכֶם לְכַף זְכוּת. וְתָלִיתִי בְּבִטּוּל תּוֹרָה; אַחַר־כָּךְ כְּשֶׁבָּאתִי לִמְקוֹמְכֶם וְלֹא בָּאתֶם אֵלַי, דַּנְתִּי אֶתְכֶם גַּם־כֵּן לְכַף זְכוּת, וְתָלִיתִי גַּם־כֵּן בְּבִטּוּל תּוֹרָה. אַחַר־כָּךְ כְּשֶׁבָּאתִי לְבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת וְלֹא נְתַתֶּם לִי שָׁלוֹם, דַּנְתִּי גַּם־כֵּן לְכַף זְכוּת, וְתָלִיתִי גַּם־כֵּן בְּבִטּוּל תּוֹרָה, שֶׁאֵין אַתֶּם רוֹצִים לְהַפְסִיק מִן הַתּוֹרָה כְּלָל. עַכְשָׁו אֲנִי רוֹאֶה שֶׁשֶּׁקֶר הוּא כִּי הֲלֹא אֶת הַבָּחוּר כִּבַּדְתֶּם וְדִבַּרְתֶּם
עִמּוֹ הַרְבֵּה בְּאֶמְצַע הַלִּמּוּד. וְכָעַס עָלָיו מְאֹד.
וְאָמַר הַמַרְשָׁ"א לְאוֹת וּלְמוֹפֵת שֶׁהַבָּחוּר הַזֶּה בְּעוֹד שְׁתֵּי שָׁעוֹת יֵהָרֵג, וְלֹא רָצָה הָרַב לְהַאֲמִין וְלָקַח אֶת הַבָּחוּר הַנַּ"ל וְהָלַךְ עִמּוֹ אַחַת הֵנָּה וְאַחַת הֵנָּה, וְדִבֵּר עִמּוֹ הַרְבֵּה הַרְבֵּה לְבַל יַנִּיחֶנּוּ לְהִתְעַלֵּם מִן הָעַיִן עַד עֲבֹר הַשְּׁתֵּי שָׁעוֹת לְהַכְחִישׁ דִּבְרֵי הַמַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל. וַיְהִי מִדֵּי עָבְרָם בָּעִיר וְחָלַף וְהָלַךְ אֶצְלָם אֵיזֶה אָדוֹן, וְהָיָה מוֹשֵׁךְ בִּקְנֵה שְׂרֵפָה (רוֹבֶה) לְפִי תֻּמּוֹ לִירוֹת אֵיזֶה עוֹף וְכַיּוֹצֵא כְּדַרְכָּם, וַיַּךְ אֶת הַבָּחוּר הַנַּ"ל וְנֶהֱרַג אַחַר שְׁתֵּי שָׁעוֹת מִיָּד כְּדִבְרֵי הַמַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל, לֹא נָפַל דָּבָר. וְרָץ הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה הַנַּ"ל וּבָא אֶל הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל וְאָמַר לוֹ הַמַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל שֶׁבְּסָמוּךְ יָבִיאוּ הָרוּג לְפֹה. בְּתוֹךְ כָּךְ שֶׁהָיוּ מְדַבְּרִים נִשְׁמַע מִיָּד שֶׁהֵבִיאוּ אֵיזֶה הָרוּג אֶל הָעִיר. אָז נִתְבַּהֵל הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה הַנַּ"ל, וְשָׁאַל לְהַמַּהַרְשָׁ"א מַה זֹּאת. אָז סִפֵּר הַמַרְשָׁ"א וְגִלָּה לוֹ כָּל הָעִנְיָן, הֱיוֹת שֶׁזֶּה הַבָּחוּר הָיָה גִּלְגּוּל אַחְאָב מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל וּמֵחֲמַת זֶה חָלַק לוֹ כָּבוֹד כָּל־כָּךְ. וּמֵחֲמַת שֶׁאַחְאָב מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל נֶהֱרַג הָיָה מֻכְרָח זֶה הַבָּחוּר לִהְיוֹת נֶהֱרָג גַּם־כֵּן. וְתֵכֶף שֶׁיָּצָא לָעוֹלָם זֶה הַבָּחוּר אֲזַי תֵּכֶף נִבְרָא מַשְׁחִית אֶחָד בִּשְׁבִיל לַהֲרֹג אֶת אוֹתוֹ הַבָּחוּר הַנַּ"ל וְהָיָה עוֹמֵד בַּמָּקוֹם הַהוּא דְּהַיְנוּ סָמוּךְ לָעִיר הַזֹּאת וְהָיָה מְצַפֶּה עַד שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ זְמַנּוֹ שֶׁל זֶה הַבָּחוּר הַנַּ"ל שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נֶהֱרַג עַל־יָדוֹ. וּמֵחֲמַת שֶׁאַתֶּם עִכַּבְתֶּם אוֹתוֹ כַּנַּ"ל, עַד שֶׁנֶּהֱרַג בְּכָאן עַל־יְדֵי הָאָדוֹן הַנַּ"ל, עַל־יְדֵי־זֶה הָיוּ מֻכְרָחִים לִתֵּן לְהַמַּשְׁחִית הַנַּ"ל אִישׁ אַחֵר בִּמְקוֹמוֹ, וְזֶה הֶהָרוּג שֶׁנֶּהֱרַג עַל־יָדוֹ. עַל־כֵּן צְרִיכִים אַתֶּם לְקַבֵּל תְּשׁוּבָה, כִּי עַל־יֶדְכֶם נֶהֱרַג זֶה הֶהָרוּג, כִּי אַתֶּם סִבַּבְתֶּם זֹאת עַל־יְדֵי הָעִכּוּב שֶׁעִכַּבְתֶּם אֶת הַבָּחוּר פֹּה כַּנַּ"ל. אָז נָפַל הָרַב דִּמְדִינָה לִפְנֵי רַגְלֵי הַמַרְשָׁ"א וּפִיֵּס אוֹתוֹ וְהִתְחַנֵּן לְפָנָיו שֶׁיִּמְחֹל לוֹ. וּבִקֵּשׁ אוֹתוֹ שֶׁיִּתֵּן לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה. וְאָמַר לוֹ הַמַרְשָׁ"א, שֶׁתְּשׁוּבָתְךָ שֶׁתְּסַלֵּק מִיָּדְךָ אֶת כֶּתֶר הָרַבָּנוּת וְתִהְיֶה בַּעַל עֲגָלָה. וְקִבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ כָּךְ, וְנַעֲשָׂה בַּעַל עֲגָלָה: וּדְבַר אֱלֹהֵינוּ יָקוּם לְעוֹלָם.

* * * *

Story 4 Kaptzin Pasha A story that our master, leader, and teacher Rabbi Nachman told over — about Kaptzin Pasha. Once by the Turkish King [Sultan] there was a man from our Jewish brethren who was very important in his eyes — more than all the royal ministers he had — and he loved him with very great and strong love. And every single day he would call him to his house to delight in his company. The royal ministers were jealous of him and schemed plots to defame him before the king so that he should eradicate him from the world. And among them there was a pasha called Kaptzin Pasha — whose hatred for this Jew was greater than all the ministers'. But in front of the Jew he presented himself as his friend — and every day he schemed plots desiring to succeed in finding some defamation against him before the king. Once the aforementioned pasha came to the aforementioned Jew — and began to speak to him slyly — and told him how he was by the king — and heard from his mouth how he loves you — "but he suffers from one thing: when you come before him to speak with him he cannot bear the odor of your mouth — for he senses a bad odor wafting from your mouth. But he cannot be without you — and he has great suffering from this. So my advice is: every time you come before the king — hold a kerchief with fragrance in front of your mouth — in order that the king will not sense the bad breath — for the fragrance will dispel the bad odor — so that you do not stink in the eyes of the king." And the aforementioned Jew — due to his temimus [innocence] — believed his words — and resolved in his mind to do so. Afterwards the aforementioned pasha went to the king and told him that he had heard from the aforementioned Jew: that he said he has great suffering — for every time he speaks with the king he senses a bad odor emanating from the king's mouth. "Therefore his resolution is that when he comes to speak with you, my master the king, he will hold a kerchief with fragrance against his mouth — in order not to sense the bad odor from the king's mouth. And this is the sign that my words are true — for tomorrow when he comes to speak with you — you will see with your own eyes that he will hold a kerchief against his mouth." When the king heard this he was very angry — and said: "When I see that your words are true — then I will abolish him from the world." And behold — the aforementioned Jew came on the morrow before the king — and held a kerchief against his mouth as the pasha had advised him — for he believed his words. And when the king saw this — it was clear in his mind that the words of the pasha were true. Immediately he wrote a letter as follows: "When the person who gives over this note comes before you — throw him immediately into the incinerator where all those sentenced for execution are burned there." And the king sealed the letter with his seal — and said to this man: "I request that you personally deliver this letter to the man written in the address — which is in such-and-such a place." And the aforementioned Jew took the letter — and promised the king he would do as he said — and did not know what was written in it — and went to his home. Now this Jewish man was avidly active in the mitzvah to circumcise Jewish children — and whenever they would honor him with the mitzvah of the cutting he would not pay attention to any hindrance — for the mitzvah was very precious in his eyes. And then — on that very day that he needed to travel to deliver the king's letter — Hashem, Who desired to save His trusted friend, brought about that someone came from a town and honored him to travel with him to the town and circumcise his son. And because his practice was not to leave this mitzvah for any reason — he began to deliberate: "What shall I do for the king's command — in the matter of his letter?" And Hashem brought about that the aforementioned pasha came before him. And he told over to the pasha: the king had given him a letter to deliver — and today Hashem had presented him with the mitzvah of cutting — and his practice was not to leave this mitzvah for any reason. "Therefore I am requesting from you that you take the letter and bring it there." Now the aforementioned pasha was very happy — for now he could slander him further before the king — that he had not carried out the king's desire with the letter. And the pasha took the letter from his hand and delivered it to the person it was being sent to — and this was the executioner appointed to burn those the king had sentenced to death. And immediately he grabbed the aforementioned pasha and threw him into the furnace — and he was burned — as he deserved to be punished by Hashem — measure for measure. Now the Jew did not know anything of what had been done to him. On the morrow he returned and came before the king. When the king saw him he was very puzzled and said to him: "Have you still not delivered the letter that I put in your hands for that aforementioned man?" He answered: "My master the king — the letter I gave over to Kaptzin Pasha to deliver — for Hashem had presented me with the mitzvah of cutting — and my practice is not to leave this mitzvah." The king then understood: is it not a phenomenon that this pasha who had slandered him should be burned? So the king immediately asked the man: "What is this — that you hold a kerchief with fragrance against your mouth when you speak with me?" He answered that the pasha had given him this remedy — "for he told me that he heard from you that you cannot bear the bad breath from my mouth." The king then told over to him how the pasha had slandered him — "that you said to him you could not bear the bad breath from my mouth — and therefore you would hold a kerchief so as not to sense the bad odor from my mouth." And the king told over what was written in the letter he had given him. And he said: "Now I know that Hashem is the ruler of the land Who saves His cherished from all evil. And to the aforementioned pasha — just as he schemed to do to you — so was done to him — and Hashem returned unto him retribution upon his head." And from then on his importance in the eyes of the king was greater than all the ministers — and he was very, very important and precious in his eyes.

* * * *

Story 5 The Flood A story of rain — regarding the matter that Hashem, may He be blessed, will conquer the battle only with the simple — those who recite Psalms with simplicity etc. — and not with those who go with wisdoms. Rebbe Nachman told over a parable of a king who went hunting — and set out dressed as a commoner so as to facilitate the amusement. In the middle — suddenly heavy rain fell — literally a flood of water. All of the ministers scattered one by one etc. — and the king was in dire danger — and he searched until he found a cottage. And there was a villager there — and he took the king in and dressed him — and gave him his food: groats [barley soup] etc. — and heated the oven and let the king sleep on its threshold. It was so sweet and pleasant for the king that he had never tasted such a taste of pleasantness — since he had been so tired and exhausted etc. The royal ministers searched for the king until they came there and saw that he was sleeping. They wanted the king to return home with them — but he told them: "Since you did not save me — rather everyone scattered to save himself — whereas this man saved me — and here I tasted such sweetness — therefore he will bring me in his wagon — with these clothes — and he will seat me on the royal throne." Rebbe Nachman concluded this: it is brought down that at the heels of the Messiah [ikevos Meshicha] there will be a flood — they will shoot with heresy — not of water — but of foreign improper thoughts. And they will cover all the towering mountains. Even in the Land of Israel — where the flood did not reach — just due to the force of their projection the waters streamed there. That is: it will splash in even into the kosher hearts. And with wisdoms no remedy will be able to be given. And all the royal ministers will scatter — and all the royalty will not hold up — vet zikh nit der haltin nor [will not hold up — only] — the simple Jews who recite Psalms with simplicity etc. Therefore when the Messiah comes — they will place the royal crown on his head. There is another version to this story — with an additional part not brought in the standard printed version. After the villager crowns the king — the king tells him: "In reward for saving me so much from death — ask something of me and I will do it." And he asked a ridiculous thing: there is a great distance from his house to Odessa — hundreds of miles — and his sons bring merchandise to Odessa and it is very laborious — a long journey taking days and years — the profit going for the trip — leaving only a small gain. "Therefore I ask that you command to make the way shorter." And the king promised him — and commanded that they make the measurement units [parsuos] longer: for example if a parsu was twenty kilometers — they should now make it forty kilometers — and thereby the way will be shorter — for in place of forty parsuos it will now be only twenty parsuos. In Rebbe Nachman's concluding words mentioned above — he added mention to this addendum: the simple Psalm-reciters who unknowingly save the King and bring him back to crown him should have the intelligence not to ask for something foolish.

מַעֲשֶׂה שֵׁנִי מֵהַמַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל. בְּאוֹסְטְרָה מְקוֹם הַמַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל הָיָה טֻמְאָה לְהַגּוֹיִים, כְּשֶׁהָיוּ הַיְּהוּדִים צְרִיכִים לֵילֵךְ עִם נִפְטָר דֶּרֶךְ הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה (כִּי לֹא הָיָה לָהֶם דֶּרֶךְ אַחֶרֶת) אָז הָיוּ מְצַלְצְלִים וְכוּ', וְכָל מִי שֶׁהָלַךְ דֶּרֶךְ שָׁם הֵמִיר דָּתוֹ רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן. וְצִוָּה הַמַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל, שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה נִפְטָר מֵהָעוֹלָם וְיִשְּׂאֻהוּ דֶּרֶךְ שָׁם, יַנִּיחוּ עָלָיו חִבּוּר הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א שֶׁעָשָׂה. וְעָשׂוּ כֵן. וְשָׁם הִתְאַסְּפוּ כָּל הַכּוֹמְרִים וְהִתְחִילוּ לְצַלְצֵל. וְהֶעֱמִידוּ אֶת מִטָּתוֹ, וַיּוֹשֶׁב הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל אֶת עַצְמוֹ וְהִתְחִיל לְדַפְדֵף אֶת הַדַּפִּים, וְהִתְחִילָה הַטֻּמְאָה עִם הָאֲנָשִׁים לְהִבָּלַע בָּאָרֶץ, וְנִבְלְעוּ כֻּלָּם בָּאָרֶץ. וְעַד הַיּוֹם יֵשׁ סִימָן מִזֶּה שֶׁנִּבְלְעָה בָּאָרֶץ.

Story 6 Ivan A parable of "who is here?" that Rebbe Nachman told over. That a man once traveled with a wagon driver — to Berlin or some other large city. The man went to attend to his needs — and the coachman — whose name was Ivan [a coarse, insensitive type] — was left with the wagon in the middle of the market. A policeman [soldier] came over to him and asked him why he was stationed there — and said to him: Ver-da? ["Who is here?"] And Ivan — thinking that the policeman was asking his name — said to him: "Ivan." And he struck him and said: Ver-da?! And he yelled: "Ivan!" And he strikes him and screams: Ver-da?! — until he took him with the wagon to a side street. When the man returned — he searched for him until he found him — and said to him: "Ivan etc." He replied in a whisper and with fear: "Do not say Ivan — just: Ver-da." After he left the city — Ivan said to him: "Now you can call me Ivan." There he was called Ver-da ["who is here?"] — and there he was called Ivan [coarse and insensitive]. Rebbe Nachman concluded: Ba mir iz ver-da — un ven men geyt aroys fun mir iz vider Ivun. [By me it is "ver-da" — that is, "who is he?" — that he knows his lowliness; and also his body [the Ivan] is refined and is called in the aspect of "who" and "what" — "ver-da" ["who is here?"]. And when they leave me — it continues to be Ivan — the material body is materialistic.]

* * * *

Story 7 Bitter Herbs A story of bitter herbs that Rebbe Nachman told over. Once a Jew and a German went wandering about together. And the Jew taught the German to make himself out to be like a Jew [since the Yiddish and German languages are similar] — and the Jews are compassionate and will have mercy on him. And since Pesach was approaching — he taught him how to conduct himself throughout the whole seder [when the homeowner invites him to the house] — that kiddush is made — the washing of the hands — only he forgot to tell him about the eating of bitter herbs [maror]. When he came to the seder he was famished from the whole day — and anticipated eating all the good things the Jew had told him. But they give him a piece of karpas [celery] in salt water — and the other customary seder items — and they recite the Haggadah. And he was already looking expectantly for the eating — and was happy that they are already eating the matzah. Suddenly they give him maror [bitter herbs] — and his mouth became pungent — and he thought that this was the feast — that this alone was what they would eat. He immediately fled — with bitterness and hunger — and thought to himself: "Cursed Jews! After the whole ceremony — this is what they give to eat." And he came to the study house and slept. Afterwards the Jew came with joyous countenance — satiated from eating and drinking — and asked him: "How was the seder for you?" He told him angrily. He said to him: "Hoy German fool! If you had waited a bit more — you would have eaten sumptuously like me." The same is true in the matter of Rebbe Nachman [and the service of Hashem]: that after all the exertion and toil until coming — drawing close to Rebbe Nachman or to the devotion of Hashem — to purify the body — a bit of maror — bitterness — is given. For the purification of the body comes with bitterness. But the person thinks that it will always be just the bitterness — only this is all there is — just the bitterness etc. — therefore he immediately flees. However when he waits a bit and endures this small bitterness of the purification of the body — then he feels afterwards all manner of vitality and delight. [And these parables — one can learn counsel from them for all matters of the service of Hashem.] This holds true in this matter of the service of Hashem — that first comes the bitterness of the refinement of the body — but afterwards one feels the vitality etc. See also Midrash Rabbah, Bereishis 66:4: "Tzadikim — their beginning is suffering and their end is harmony. And the evildoers have the opposite."

מַעֲשֶׂה שְׁלִישִׁי מֵהַמַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל. בְּעֵת שֶׁבָּנוּ בֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת בְּאוֹסְטְרָה וְהָיוּ צְרִיכִים כֶּסֶף רַב לִבְנוֹתוֹ, וְעַל־כֵּן עָשׂוּ הַנָּחַת אֶבֶן הַפִּנָּה בְּקָהָל רַב. וְהִכְרִיזוּ לִמְכֹּר אֶת הַנָּחַת אֶבֶן הַפִּנָּה, עַד שֶׁגְּבִיר אֶחָד קָנָה אֶת זֶה בְּשַׂק מָלֵא זְהוּבִים. וְאַחַר־כָּךְ כִּבֵּד אֶת הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל שֶׁהוּא יַנִּיחַ אֶת הָאֶבֶן. וְאָמַר לוֹ הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א שֶׁיְּבַקֵּשׁ מִמֶּנּוּ אֵיזֶה דָּבָר בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה וּבִקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לוֹ בֵּן כְּהַמַרְשָׁ"א, וְעָנָה לוֹ הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א שֶׁזֶּה קָשֶׁה מְאֹד וְשֶׁיְּבַקֵּשׁ דָּבָר אַחֵר, וְהוּא הִתְעַקֵּשׁ דַּוְקָא בְּזֶה הַדָּבָר. וְאָמַר לוֹ הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א אִם־כֵּן כְּשֶׁתַּהַר אִשְׁתְּךָ תָּמוּת אַתָּה, וּכְשֶׁתֵּלֵד תָּמוּת הִיא גַּם־כֵּן. וַאֲנִי אֲקַבֵּל אֶת הַיֶּלֶד וַאֲגַדְּלוֹ אֶצְלִי. וְהִסְכִּימוּ עַל זֶה. וְכֵן הֲוָה, וְנִתְגַּדֵּל אֵצֶל הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל. וְהָיָה נִסְתָּר, שֶׁלֹּא רָאוּ אֶצְלוֹ שׁוּם גַּדְלוּת. וְלִפְנֵי פְּטִירַת הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א צִוָּה שֶׁהוּא יְמַלֵּא מְקוֹמוֹ, וְכֵן הֲוָה. וְהָרַב הַזֶּה לֹא יָצָא לְשׁוּם לְוָיָה מֵחֲשׁוּבֵי הָעִיר, וְהָיָה קָשֶׁה בְּעֵינֵי הַקָּהָל וְהוֹכִיחוּ אוֹתוֹ עַל זֶה. וְאָמַר לְהַמְשַׁמֵּשׁ כַּאֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה לְוָיָה מֵרָאשֵׁי הַקָּהָל יִקְרָא אוֹתוֹ, וְכֵן הֲוָה, וַיֵּצֵא הָרַב וְנָטָה בְּמַפָּה עַל הַמִּטָּה, וְרָאוּ כֻּלָּם אֵיךְ הַמַּלְאֲכֵי חַבָּלָה חָטְפוּ אֶת הַנִּפְטָר מֵהַמִּטָּה וְכוּ'. וְאָמַר לָהֶם אִם־כֵּן הוּא מְהַחֲשׁוּבִים שֶׁלָּכֶם, אֵיךְ אַתֶּם רוֹצִים שֶׁאֵלֵךְ לְלַוּוֹתָם. וּמֵאָז הִכִּירוּ כֻּלָּם גְּדֻלָּתוֹ
שֶׁהוּא רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת בִּמְקוֹם הַמַהַרְשָׁ"א זַ"ל.

Story 8 The Treasure Under the Bridge A story he told of the treasure that is under the bridge. That once there was a man from a certain city who dreamt that in Vienna — under the bridge — there is a treasure. Therefore he traveled there and stood by the bridge and sought out a contrivance — what to do. For in the day he was unable due to the people. And a soldier passed by there and said to him: "What are you standing and contemplating?" He thought in his mind that it would be good to tell him — in order that he would help him and they would divide it between them. He told him the whole matter. The soldier spoke up and said to him: "Ay — a Jew gives consideration to a dream? In that case — I also dreamt that in such and such a place — by such and such a person" — and he mentioned the city of the man and the name of this man — "in the closet there is a treasure — will I travel there?" So the man traveled to his house and dug in his closet — and found the treasure. And he said afterwards: "Now I know: the treasure is by me — but in order for me to know of the treasure — it was necessary to travel to Vienna." So it is in the matter of serving Hashem: the treasure is by each one by himself — but in order to know of the treasure — one must travel to the Tzadik.

* * * *

Story 9 The Turkey Prince The parable about the turkey. Once a prince fell into a psychosis that he was a bird called a turkey — and it was required of him to sit naked underneath the table and drag bits of bread and bones like a turkey. All the doctors despaired of helping him and healing him from this — and the king was extremely distressed. Until a sage came along and said: "I take upon myself to heal him!" He too undressed himself naked — and sat underneath the table next to the aforementioned prince — and also dragged crumbs and bones. The prince asked him: "Who are you and what are you doing here?" He answered: "And what are you doing here?" He said: "I'm a turkey." He said: "I'm also a turkey." The two of them sat together like that for some time — until they became familiar with each other. Then the sage signaled — and they threw them a shirt. The sage-turkey said to the prince: "You think a turkey cannot go with a shirt? It is possible to wear a shirt and even still be a turkey!" So they both put on a shirt. After some time he signaled — and they threw them pants. And he said to him again as before: "You think that with pants it is not possible to be a turkey etc." — and they donned pants. And so with the other clothing. Afterwards he signaled — and they threw them human food from the table — and he said: "You think that if one eats good foods one is no longer a turkey?" — Men ken esn un oykh zayn hindik. [One can eat and still be a turkey.] And they ate. Afterwards he said: "You think that a turkey must specifically be under the table? It is possible to be a turkey and be by the table." And so he dealt with him until he healed him completely. There is a version with the following addition: "And this is the aspect of what our Sages ob"m said on the verse [Kings I 5:11]: 'And he became more wise than all mankind' — even from the fools." The referent is understandable to those with understanding. (The transcriber says: It is possible to say that a person who desires to draw close to the service of Hashem — behold he is a turkey dressed in materialism etc. And in this fashion it is possible — little by little — to draw himself close to the service of Hashem — until one enters completely. And so with the outreach to people in this fashion. And this is sufficient for the wise. Also see Words of Rabbi Nachman, article 67.)

הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁסִּפֵּר רַבֵּנוּ זַ"ל שֶׁבִּזְמַן הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב זַ"ל הָיָה מְנַגֵּן (כְּלֶעזְמֶר) אֶחָד שֶׁהָיָה עִוֵּר, וְהָיָה מְנַגֵּן עַל הַחֲתֻנּוֹת וְזֶה הָיְתָה פַּרְנָסָתוֹ, וְאַחַר פְּטִירָתוֹ נִתְוַדְּעוּ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה עִוֵּר כְּלָל וְהָיָה לוֹ עֵינַיִם טוֹבוֹת, וְרַק כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִסְתַּכֵּל בְּנָשִׁים עָשָׂה
עַצְמוֹ כָּל יְמֵי חַיָּיו כְּעִוֵּר וְכָל הָעוֹלָם חֲשָׁבוּהוּ לְעִוֵּר.
וְעוֹד הָיָה אִישׁ אֶחָד גְּבִיר גָּדוֹל, שֶׁהָיָה קַמְצָן גָּדוֹל שֶׁלֹּא נָתַן אֲפִלּוּ פְּרוּסַת לֶחֶם לִצְדָקָה, וְהָיָה נִבְזֶה בְּעֵינֵי כֻּלָּם בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה, וְהָיָה אָז אֶחָד בַּעַל צְדָקָה גָּדוֹל, שֶׁהָיָה מַחֲזִיק כָּל הָעֲנִיִּים בַּאֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה וְכָל מַחְסוֹרָם וְכוּ'. וְהִנֵּה כַּאֲשֶׁר נִפְטַר הַגְּבִיר הַנַּ"ל, שֶׁכֻּלָּם בִּזּוּ אוֹתוֹ מֵחֲמַת קַמְצָנוּתוֹ. וּלְמָחֳרָתוֹ כְּשֶׁהָלְכוּ הָעֲנִיִּים לְהַבַּעַל צְדָקָה הַנַּ"ל שֶׁיְּפַרְנְסֵם, עָנָה לָהֶם שֶׁעַכְשָׁו אֵין לוֹ מַה לִּתֵּן לָהֶם, שֶׁהַכֹּל מַה שֶּׁנָּתַן לָהֶם כָּל הַזְּמַן, הָיָה רַק שֶׁל זֶה הַגְּבִיר הַקַּמְצָן שֶׁמֵּת, וְלֹא רָצָה לֵהָנוֹת מֵהַכָּבוֹד שֶׁיִּתְּנוּ לוֹ עַל נְדִיבוּת לִבּוֹ, וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַמִּצְוָה נְקִיָּה בְּלִי פְּנִיּוֹת לָכֵן הָיָה נוֹתֵן אֶת הַצְּדָקוֹת לָאִישׁ הַזֶּה שֶׁיְּחַלְּקֵם, וְאוֹתוֹ חָשְׁבוּ כֻּלָּם לְקַמְצָן גָּדוֹל. וְעַכְשָׁו שֶׁמֵּת אֵין מִי שֶׁיִּתֵּן,
וְאָז יָדְעוּ כֻּלָּם גְּדֻלָּתוֹ.
וְאָמַר הַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב זַ"ל, שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם הַמְנַגֵּן הָעִוֵּר הַנַּ"ל וְהַגְּבִיר הַקַּמְצָן הַזֶּה שְׁנֵיהֶם הֵם בְּמַדְרֵגָה אַחַת. וְזָכוּ לְמַה
שֶּׁזָּכוּ, אַשְׁרֵי לָהֶם.
